title: the lac house
hook: the city starts calling Yudhishthira its future king, and Duryodhana makes his father an offer: a holiday in Varanavata

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Karna's abandonment: a crown, a bow to the old charioteer, and an insult at sunset — it follows him into every room. Did you ask someone what they love before where they're from? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

Talk in the streets of Hastinapura: in squares and courtyards, people are saying Yudhishthira should be king. He's fair, they say, he's truthful, he's Pandu's eldest. Dhritarashtra is blind, so he was passed over before; why should his line rule now? Word of it reaches Duryodhana, and it burns. The Mahabharata gives him a long, anguished speech to his father. If Yudhishthira takes the throne, the crown will pass down his line, and we and our children will be shut out and disregarded. Today begins the lac house, and it begins with gossip.
screen: `THE STREETS TALK.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA SHOULD BE KING.` → `DURYODHANA BURNS.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana has a plan, and it's dressed up as a kindness. Send the Pandavas away, he tells his father, to the town of Varanavata, where a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva, is under way. Let them enjoy themselves for a while. Out of the capital, out of the people's eyes. Dhritarashtra hesitates. Pandu was good to me, he says, and the people love his sons; how can I do this? But he loves his own son, and in the end he agrees. So the old king calls his nephews in and speaks warmly about Varanavata: what a lovely town, what a festival, go and enjoy it. Yudhishthira sees the purpose behind it, the text says, but he's alone and without friends at court, and he agrees. Then Duryodhana calls a minister named Purochana, and gives him the real job. Go ahead to Varanavata. Build a fine house for the Pandavas. Build it out of lac and resin and other things that burn, and plaster it over so it looks like any house. Treat them well. Earn their trust. And one night, when they're asleep, set it on fire. Notice the shape of the plot. Nothing is done in the open. A father is persuaded. A holiday is offered. A house is built with care. Every step looks generous. That's the lac house before a single wall goes up: a trap made of kindness. And it can't happen without the blind king, who hesitated, and then said yes.
screen: `SEND THEM ON A HOLIDAY.` · `THE BLIND KING HESITATES.` · `PUROCHANA'S REAL JOB.` · `A HOUSE BUILT TO BURN.` · then, large: `A TRAP MADE OF KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the breath slow. Recall a time you went along with something you suspected wasn't right, because it was easier, or because someone you loved wanted it. Don't scold yourself. Just look at the moment honestly, the way the story looks at Dhritarashtra. Where did you feel the hesitation? Notice that place now. The bell holds the time.
Purochana, the minister Duryodhana trusted to build a house of lac and resin in Varanavata, and to set it aflame.
Your line: a trap made of kindness. Today, when an offer seems too generous, ask quietly what it's made of. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: The bait in this story is a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva; Hindus still worship Shiva as Pashupati, and the Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu carries the name.

myth: he hesitated, remembering Pandu's goodness and the people's love for his sons, then gave in to his own son.
the house was meant to look ordinary
built of lac and resin and other things that burn, plastered over to look like any house.
Purochana was told to treat the Pandavas harshly
he was told to treat them well and earn their trust, and burn the house while they slept.

fork.setup: you're Dhritarashtra. your son begs you to send your nephews away. you remember how good their father was to you. what do you do?
options: agree, and send them to Varanavata.
tell your nephews what your son wants.
fork.reveal: he hesitates, but agrees. he sends the Pandavas off with warm words about a festival.

original.note: Sanskrit lākṣāgṛha: the house of lac, built to burn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a house that catches fire by accident.
what it means: a house planned to burn, offered as a kindness, with every step of the plot made to look generous.
what a scholar hears: the plot needs the blind king's consent, and the text shows him hesitating before he gives it.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (the citizens praise Yudhishthira; Duryodhana's appeal; Dhritarashtra sends the Pandavas to Varanavata; Purochana's commission)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli the citizens' talk, Duryodhana's argument to his father, and Dhritarashtra's hesitation (Pandu's goodness, the people's love).

Confirm the materials named for the house (lac, resin, hemp, mixed with earth and ghee; the script names only lac and resin) and Purochana's instructions to win their trust and burn the house while they sleep.
The counsel of Kanika is left out; a Keeper may want it included on a neighboring day.

Editor pass: Duryodhana's 'rule forever' and 'living on their charity' brought closer to the text (excluded and disregarded); named the festival of Pashupati and gave Yudhishthira's reason for agreeing (he perceives the motive but is friendless; confirm both in Ganguli); practice opener varied; generic howItsDone replaced with Shiva as Pashupati.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): checked against the Jatugriha Parva (citizens' talk, Dhritarashtra's hesitation, the Pashupati festival, Yudhishthira weak and friendless, Purochana's orders); no changes needed. Kanika's counsel still omitted, as noted.
